title: How the American Federation for Teachers Could be a Positive force in an AI World
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: Bauschard criticizes the AFT's promotion of an AI writing detector as a control tool that is inaccurate, biased against ELL and special education students, and easily defeated. He reads the decision as part of a wider attempt by educators to retain control of instruction and information while students can learn anything anywhere, increasingly from AI. His claim is that decentralization through online schools, micro-schools and AI tutors will shrink enrollment and threaten teacher employment regardless of what schools decide. He compares the moment to librarians resisting Wikipedia, and says human teachers keep a role in encouragement and moral guidance but not in content control. The constructive turn is to urge the union to fund AI literacy training and help build networked, decentralized models of schooling.
points: AI writing detectors are inaccurate and biased against ELL and special education students, undercutting the AFT's stated values of fairness and opportunity.
Teacher jobs are threatened less by schools adopting AI tutors than by families leaving conventional schools for decentralized options.
Defending teachers as controllers of information is a lost cause, comparable to librarians fighting Wikipedia.
Human teachers retain love, encouragement and moral guidance, while AI beats them on content, availability and individualization.
The AFT could instead provide AI literacy training and help shape networked models of schooling.
quotes: There is overwhelming evidence that these detectors are not accurate and biased against students with more predictable writing skills, including ELL learners and special education students, undermining two of the core values the AFT claims to stand for: fairness and opportunity.
Decentralization of education clearly threatens the jobs of public educators. I’ll unpack this more in a future post, but we can already see this trend.

Human teachers will be able to offer many things that AI teachers cannot (love, encouragement, moral guidance, and needed human social and emotional interventions), but AIs will be able to surpass most teachers in other areas (content knowledge (relative to AIs that have solved the hallucination issue and at least one has in teaching), 24/7 availability, ability to produce individual assignments, ability to adjust instruction to the individual rather than the group, etc.). Remember that they are already choosing to spend time with their AIs rather than their teachers.
And this will be magnified if educators continue to focus their roles on teaching content and managing and controlling information. AIs can do that, and they are really awesome at it.
We’ve seen this rodeo before. We can remember back to the early 2000s when librarians fought hard against Wikipedia, arguing it was unreliable.

The AFT made a huge bet on a control tool that doesn’t function properly, that the kids (at least the high SES kids) know how to defeat, and that they can pay another tool to defeat. This is a lost cause.

The AFT could play a positive role by providing more than lip service to the idea of providing essential AI literacy training that teachers desperately need to work in an AI World and which is currently not being provided by most schools.
